text: Quantum speedup gets talked about as if it's one single thing, but it actually comes in at least three very different flavors — and knowing which flavor applies to a given problem is what separates a real, precise claim from marketing.

Shor's algorithm gives an exponential speedup: it factors in time polynomial in the bit length on a quantum computer, against a sub-exponential best classical algorithm. Grover's algorithm gives a quadratic speedup: roughly root N oracle queries instead of N. And for the overwhelming majority of computational problems, no quantum algorithm offering any advantage at all is known. Telling these three apart for a given problem is the actual skill this course is building.

Here's Grover's quadratic speedup with real numbers. Searching one million unsorted items classically needs up to one million checks in the worst case. Grover's algorithm needs only floor of pi over four times the square root of one million, which works out to exactly 785 oracle queries. That's a huge practical win — but notice N is still inside the square root, not in the exponent. That's what makes it quadratic, not exponential.

Every speedup claim is relative to something. Grover's is measured against a query model, a clean mathematical result about oracle calls. Shor's is measured against the best classical algorithm anyone has found so far, the General Number Field Sieve — not against a proof that no faster classical algorithm could ever exist. That's exactly why complexity theorists say factoring is believed, not proven, to be hard classically. And it's why quantum computers are faster at everything is a myth directly contradicted by complexity theory: if it were true, BQP would have to contain NP, and no evidence supports that.
Next lesson puts all of this into practice: a repeatable four-question checklist, worked through on four real problems, so you can classify something you've never seen before.
